trajectory_summary: The call opens cold with an accidental-tap admission and an immediate affordability objection, but the rep keeps momentum by pivoting quickly into verify questions and the bill-swap pitch. The back half is dominated by a long, clumsy bill-retrieval process that the customer works through mostly on her own, and the call closes with a booked phone appointment but a rushed, garbled button-up. Overall shape is mixed: real engagement was built through the customer's own persistence, not through strong rep technique.

observed_outcome.quote: Alright. So we got you for the twentieth at 1PM.
observed_outcome.reasoning: A specific day (the twentieth) and time (1PM) are confirmed for a phone call appointment; no co-owner/spouse was identified on this call since the customer is sole trustee, so co_owner_confirmed is not applicable.

bill_anchor_audit.bill_quote: Usually, the total bill is around 500 or more, sometimes close to 6.
bill_anchor_audit.reasoning: The rep acknowledges the number ('We could definitely help with that') but never turns it into an explicit reason to act or ties it back to her stated fixed-income fear; the flip should have landed right after 03:18 or again at 07:24 when she volunteered the 25.69% increase.

interest_reason_audit.reasoning: The rep asked a leading yes/no version of the interest question ('your interest in solar is saving money?') rather than an open one, and the customer's flat confirmation was never reinforced later — for example, not tied back to the appointment or to her later bill-increase disclosure at 07:24.

primary_coaching_focus.topic: curiosity creation on customer-volunteered pain data
primary_coaching_focus.quote: Right. And that says my bill is 25.69% higher than last year, the March.
primary_coaching_focus.why: This is the richest anchor point in the entire call — the customer did the rep's job for him by surfacing her own bill-pain number — and the rep let it pass with a passive acknowledgment instead of tying it to the appointment's value, the single highest-leverage miss on this call.

key_moments.quote: So are you looking for solar or no?
key_moments.stewart_read: The rep never establishes company legitimacy, lead source detail, or state framing before jumping to a blunt interest check. This skips the 'is this a scam?' reassurance the intro is supposed to provide.

key_moments.quote: I don't probably can't can't afford it. I'm on a fixed income.
key_moments.stewart_read: This is a textbook cost objection early in the call. The rep pitches the bill-swap program (a reasonable response) but never explicitly flips the framing to 'what you can't afford is your current bill' — the inversion move stays implicit rather than stated.

key_moments.quote: Are you the only one on the title?
key_moments.stewart_read: The customer discloses a trust structure ('Piazza Trust') with herself as trustee — an unusual ownership form the rep accepts at face value without probing whether other trustees/beneficiaries have decision authority.

key_moments.quote: Well, I do you have a shingle roof?
key_moments.stewart_read: The rep runs the roof-type verify item but garbles the phrasing badly enough that the customer has to ask for clarification, costing time and slightly undermining the rep's polish.
